short: The European Code of Conduct on Data Centre Energy Efficiency is a voluntary programme run by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre since 2008; Participants commit to the expected practices in the annual Best Practice Guidelines (latest 2025 edition, March 2025) and Endorsers support it; it is not a certification.
title: EU Code of Conduct for Data Centres (Energy Efficiency)
subtitle: The European Commission JRC's voluntary energy efficiency programme for data centers
body_html:
What the EU Code of Conduct for Data Centres is

The European Code of Conduct on Data Centre Energy Efficiency is a voluntary initiative run by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC). The JRC says it was created in 2008 in response to rising energy use in data centers and the environmental, economic and energy supply security impacts that follow. Organisations that take part commit to adopting energy management best practices in their data centers.

The practices are set out in the Best Practice Guidelines, revised each year. The latest edition the JRC repository lists is the 2025 Best Practice Guidelines for the EU Code of Conduct on Data Centre Energy Efficiency (JRC141521, EUR 40267), published 21 March 2025.

What it covers

The Best Practice Guidelines are the full list of recognised energy efficiency practices under the Code, with a common terminology. Earlier editions group them into areas including data center management and planning, IT equipment and services, cooling, power equipment, other data center equipment, the building, and monitoring and reporting of energy use.

A subset of practices is marked as the expected minimum for Participant status. Some apply to the whole existing data center; others apply when new IT equipment or software is deployed, or when a facility is built or significantly refitted. Remaining practices are optional.

How a claim is made and checked

The Code has two roles:

  • Participant: an operator that applies for Participant status for its data center, implements the expected practices and reports through the Code's reporting form. Where an expected practice cannot be applied, the Participant explains why in the form and may name an equivalent practice. The Best Practices form part of the application and assessment for Participant status, which the JRC secretariat handles.
  • Endorser: the role of supporting and promoting the Code's practices rather than implementing them. The JRC says an operator that does not control the whole data center, such as a colocation provider that does not run its customers' IT, signs as a Participant and acts as an Endorser for the practices outside its control, for example by actively endorsing the IT practices to its customers.

Data centers that achieve Participant status are listed on the Code of Conduct website with their operator type.

What a claim does not mean

  • Participation is voluntary and is not a certification. The Code has no audit by an accredited body; the JRC secretariat reviews applications.
  • Participant status means the operator committed to the expected practices and reports to the JRC. It does not mean a particular PUE or efficiency level has been reached.
  • Endorser status is support for the Code, not operation of a data center to its practices.
  • The JRC says practice values (1 to 5) are qualitative and are not meant to be added up into an operator score.

In data centers

Participant status is granted per data center, so a claim should name the sites. A reader should check whether the operator is a Participant or only an Endorser, which data centers are listed, and which year's Best Practice Guidelines apply. The JRC says customers and IT service suppliers can ask for a list of the Code of Conduct practices implemented in a data center when buying services with sustainability requirements. The JRC also says the 2025 guidelines serve as a reference for the EU Taxonomy Delegated Act on climate mitigation in data centres, and are mentioned in Article 12 of the 2023 Energy Efficiency Directive.

Related standards

The Code's practices are mapped in CENELEC's maturity model CLC/TS 50600-5-1 (see EN 50600). Operators often pair it with ISO 50001 energy management and the Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact.

Primary sources
